lines.trans: This playground has been right here ever since I was little.
I used to play here a lot too.
I played here all the time with Joon-mo.
Ye-jin, are you going to stay upset like this forever?
Would you feel happy if our house became yours—do not use my room carelessly!
My grandmother always said if you cry, more and more things to cry about will happen.
Now I am telling you all sorts of personal stories.
Did I not tell you that whenever you want to confide in someone and have nobody to tell, you can tell me?
Look how grown-up you sound, Baek Seung-chan—still, your phone keeps ringing, is it okay to stay out this long?
Ah yes, I will head back right away!

meanings.note: demonstrative determiner placed before a noun

examples.text: 이 바닥은 자기 밥그릇은 자기가 챙겨야 돼.
examples.trans: In this industry, you have to look after your own rice bowl.
This book is interesting.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 이 놀이터 나 어렸을 때 옛날부터 있던 건데.
examples.trans: This playground has been right here ever since I was little.
Here the word for 'playground' is key.

meanings.note: Plain first-person singular pronoun used with friends, younger people, or subordinates; contracts to 난 with -는 and becomes 내가 before -가.

examples.trans: I'm going to stay home today.
I'll go first.
It really is was young compared to what I thought.
Especially today, it is was young and nice.

meanings.note: Often used as a bound noun after -(으)ㄹ to mean 'when' or 'while'.

examples.trans: Call me when you have time.
I lived in this neighborhood when I was young.

meanings.en: the old days, old times, the past

examples.trans: In the old days, this neighborhood was quiet.
Sometimes I think of the old days.

있다.gloss: to exist, to have, to stay

meanings.en: to exist, to be (in a place)
meanings.note: Opposite of 없다.
Marks the possessed item with 이/가.

examples.trans: Do you have time?
Nobody is at home.

related.gloss: to not exist, to not have

meanings.note: Bound noun often contracted to 거 in everyday speech.

examples.trans: This is my bag.
Because I think I'm late.

meanings.note: Humble first-person singular pronoun used in polite speech.

examples.trans: I have an induction ceremony.
Follow me.

meanings.note: Often used directly without a locative particle to mean 'here'.

examples.trans: Please sit here.
Here is our office.

meanings.en: a lot, much, in large quantity
meanings.note: Adverbial form of 많다 (to be many/much)

examples.trans: I did a lot of work today.
Please eat plenty and enjoy.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.trans: I used to play here a lot too.
This expression comes from 'used to play'.

examples.text: 네가 계속 메시지 남겼다는 얘기 들었어.
examples.trans: I heard that you kept leaving messages for me.
Are we just going to keep climbing this mountain like this?

meanings.note: Adverbial form of 이렇다.
Used to emphasize degree.

examples.trans: You can do it like this.
Why is it so cold today?

meanings.note: commonly paired with 좋다 ('good') or 나쁘다 ('bad')

examples.trans: The weather is clear, so I'm in a good mood.

examples.text: 칭찬을 들으니 기분이 날아갈 것 같아요.
examples.trans: Hearing the compliment makes me feel on cloud nine.

meanings.note: Short-form negation placed directly before verbs and adjectives

examples.trans: I'm not going to the office today.
I haven't watched that movie yet.

좋다.gloss: to be good, to be nice

examples.trans: I feel really good today.
It's nice to take a walk in the morning.
Do you have time today?
Where are you going?

meanings.note: Used only with close friends, younger people, or children
Used in -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 to express 'it seems that...' or 'I think...'.

meanings.en: to be the same, to be like
meanings.note: Compares two things with -와/과 같다.

examples.trans: I think I'm late.
It looks like it's going to rain.

meanings.note: 1st person plural pronoun; also used for 'my' with family, school, or workplace

examples.trans: Our team has a good atmosphere.
Let's eat lunch together tomorrow.
I'm on my way home right now.
On weekends I usually rest at home.
Did you hear about this you guys?
I was busy today because of you guys.

meanings.note: Takes a complement marked with 이/가.

examples.trans: I want to become a doctor.
It has already become 12 o'clock.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 너 같으면 좋겠냐? 우리 집이 너희 집 됐는데, 내 방 함부로 쓰지 마!
examples.trans: Would you feel happy if our house became yours—do not use my room carelessly!
Here the word for 'room' is key.

meanings.note: Adverb describing acting or speaking without proper thought, caution, or respect. RR: hamburo.

examples.trans: Do not touch other people's things carelessly.
You must not make promises lightly.

meanings.note: Irregular ㅡ-stem verb: 쓰다 + -어 becomes 써.
Commonly used for tools, money, or time.

examples.trans: I write in my diary every night.
I wrote my name on the very first page of the book.

meanings.note: Auxiliary verb used after -지 to tell someone not to do something. Ending with -고 (말고) gives a brisk, trailing command. RR: malda.

examples.trans: Please do not worry.
Do not be late, and come early.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 우리 할머니가 그랬어, 울면 자꾸만 더 울 일이 생긴다고.
examples.trans: My grandmother always said if you cry, more and more things to cry about will happen.
Here the word for 'grandmother' is key.

그러다.gloss: to say so; to do so

meanings.en: to say so; to speak like that
meanings.note: contracted from 그러하다; often follows quoted speech

meanings.en: to do so; to act like that

examples.trans: Who said that?
That friend also said they are going together.

meanings.note: ㄹ-irregular verb: ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ (e.g. 우세요, 웁니다).

examples.trans: I cried because the movie was sad.
The baby is crying loudly.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adv).

examples.text: 우리 할머니가 그랬어, 울면 자꾸만 더 울 일이 생긴다고.
examples.trans: My grandmother always said if you cry, more and more things to cry about will happen.
Here the word for 'over and over' is key.

meanings.note: Used before adjectives or verbs.

examples.trans: Please give me a little more.
It's further away.

meanings.note: Sino-Korean numeral used with counters and in numbers

examples.trans: Let's meet in the first-floor lobby.

examples.text: 일 호선이 가장 오래된 지하철 노선이에요.
examples.trans: Line 1 is the oldest subway line.
I want to end up right now.
How about trying to end up together tomorrow?

meanings.note: Emphasizes a change of state or that a new moment has arrived (contrasting with 지금 'right this second').

examples.trans: I have to go home now.
The performance is starting very soon now.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (det).

examples.text: 내가 이제 너한테 별 얘기를 다 한다.
examples.trans: Now I am telling you all sorts of personal stories.
Here the word for 'all kinds of' is key.

meanings.note: dummy

examples.trans: dummy trans 1
dummy trans 2

meanings.note: Placed before the verb it modifies.

examples.trans: I finished all my homework.
I ate all the rice.

meanings.en: to do, to perform, to hold
meanings.note: Core verb; also combines with nouns to form verbs.

examples.trans: What are you doing right now?
We are holding a meeting today.

meanings.note: interrogative pronoun; becomes 누가 before subject particle -가
indefinite pronoun

examples.trans: Did someone come outside?
Who is that person?

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.text: 내가 진짜 힘든 건, 내가 누구 좋아하면 너한테 다 털어놨었잖아.
examples.trans: What is truly hard for me is that whenever I liked someone, I used to spill everything to you.
This expression comes from 'used to confide, remember'.

meanings.note: Auxiliary adjective attached to a verb stem with -고 (-고 싶다).

examples.trans: I want to go to Korea.
I want to drink a cup of coffee.

meanings.note: Can refer to a single person or people/a crowd in general without a plural suffix.

examples.trans: There are many people in the cafeteria.
He is a good person.

없다.gloss: to not exist, to not have

meanings.en: to not exist, to not be present

examples.trans: I don't have time right now.
The tickets are all sold out, so there aren't any.
I want to humbly tell him right now.
How about trying to humbly tell him together tomorrow?

않다.gloss: to not do, to not be

meanings.en: to not do, to not be
meanings.note: Auxiliary negative verb/adjective used after -지 (long-form negation)

examples.trans: The weather isn't cold today.
I didn't say anything.
It really is is loud, so compared to what I thought.
Especially today, it is is loud, so and nice.

meanings.note: Colloquial contraction of 그런데; introduces a contrast or obstacle.
Used to shift the topic in conversation.

examples.trans: By the way, what time is it now?
I want to go. But I don't have time.

meanings.note: Sino-Korean word for telephone.

examples.trans: A phone call came.
I will hang up the phone.

meanings.en: to come (of a feeling, state, or weather)
meanings.note: Used in expressions like 혼란이 오다 (confusion comes) or 비가 오다 (rain falls)

examples.text: 한국에 온 지 일 년 됐어요.
examples.trans: It's been one year since I came to Korea.
I suddenly started feeling sleepy.
I understand well (for a long time).
Today is a (for a long time) busy day.

meanings.note: Expresses sudden realization, surprise, or hesitation.

examples.trans: Ah, yes.
Oh, I see!

meanings.note: Slightly more formal/deferential variant of 네, commonly used when speaking to a boss or superior.

examples.trans: Yes, understood.
Yes, I will prepare it right away.

meanings.note: With future or present-progressive verbs, means 'right away / in a moment'.
With past-tense verbs, means 'just now'.

examples.trans: I'll be right there.
I just arrived a moment ago.
I want to went inside right now.
How about trying to went inside together tomorrow?

meanings.note: Used in standard farewells 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Goodbye! (to someone leaving)

meanings.note: Basic verb of motion. With the respectful ending -세요 in 안녕히 가세요, it forms the polite farewell 'Goodbye!'. RR: gada.

examples.trans: I am going home.
Go safely!
